argument: Nietzsche observes that, unlike questions with obvious answers (why do I have eyeballs), the question of life's meaning has no default answer, so cultures have always invented 'true world theories' -- Plato's forms, Christian heaven, Brahman -- that posit a superior, 'true' reality beyond this flawed one to make existence bearable. Rather than trying to disprove these theories point by point, Nietzsche instead exposes the psychological incentive behind inventing them, and declares that 'God is dead' not in triumph but in mourning, since humanity has lost its ready-made answer to meaning and morality. He then turns this lens on Christianity's 'slave morality,' which he argues relabels natural urges and weakness as virtue, and on modern numbing agents like alcohol, which he sees as functioning exactly like the religious comfort he critiques.
keyIdeas: Questions like 'why do I have eyeballs' don't trouble people because everyday experience reinforces an obvious answer, but 'what is the meaning of my life' has no such default answer, which is why the question is so persistent.

'True world theories' -- Plato's world of forms, the Christian heaven, Brahman -- all share the same structure: two realities, one inferior or illusory, and one 'true' reality worth striving toward, invented the way every culture independently invented ways to carry heavy things.

Nietzsche doesn't try to disprove God the way Anselm's or Aquinas's critics tried to disprove specific proofs; instead he points out the psychological incentive people have for inventing comforting stories, and 'God is dead' is a mournful statement about losing humanity's shared answer to meaning, not a triumphant one.

Nietzsche reframes envy as a useful signal of the gap between who you are and who you want to be, and criticizes Christianity's 'slave morality' for teaching people to reject natural urges and relabel weakness and passivity as virtues.

Nietzsche calls Christianity and alcohol 'two great narcotics' because both numb people to their real shortcomings with false comfort rather than helping them grow, which is why he wouldn't be surprised that Alcoholics Anonymous works by leaning on the same higher-power mechanism.

terms.def: A worldview positing a superior, 'true' reality beyond this flawed physical one, invented to cope with the absence of an obvious meaning to life.
Nietzsche's mournful declaration that humanity has lost its shared, objective basis for meaning and morality, not a literal or triumphant claim about atheism.
Nietzsche's term for the Christian moral code that relabels weakness, passivity, and obedience as virtues.
For Nietzsche, a useful psychological signal highlighting the gap between who you are and who you want to become, usable as guidance for growth.
Something that numbs people to their real problems and shortcomings by making them feel resolved without actually resolving them, as he says of both Christianity and alcohol.
